newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stock, bond futures fall in early trade.
newsitem.headline: French stock, bond futures fall in early trade.

text.p: French stock, bond and interest rate futures fell in pre-session electronic trading on Monday after the Socialist-led left won an upset parliamentary election triumph on Sunday.

Traders said investors stopped short of panic selling, though admitted some surprise at the election result, which showed the Socialists would have to rely on the Communists to form a government, and predicted most market falls.
The franc fell to a low of 3.3860 per mark, its lowest level this year, compared to 3.3835 per mark late on Sunday.
June CAC-40 stock market futures opened 82 points lower at 2,475 and immediately fell further, dropping as low as 2,456, over four percent. At 0630 GMT they had recovered to 2,479.
June PIBOR and bond futures were lower, but holding above lows set last week after the left surprised investors and won the first round of voting.
June PIBOR futures started at 96.22, off 14 basis points, then traded down to 96.20, while the June notionnel contract was off 56 ticks at 127.94 after opening at 128.38.
"The result hasn't really impacted, we're not there yet," a bond futures trader at a French bank said. "I think it will be weaker when the pit session starts."

"Some say (the result is) already priced in. I don't think so at all. The implications of a Socialist government have not been fully taken on board, expansionist policies are not bond friendly," he said.
"This is pretty surprising," said a stock market trader in Paris. "I don't know if we're going to go lower but the CAC is getting very, very cheap."
He said much of the pressure in pre-session trading was from overseas investors, afraid of the presence of Communists in the combined left majority.
"One hundred points is a lot after last week's drop," another stock trader said. "Especially since last week's drop was made with the knowledge that the left would probably win."
"There is an emotional side to this," he added. "It is also a lot of foreign investors shifting position. People who were long and don't want to be long anymore."
